303401.text: A mosquito net positioned over a $7 \text{ ft} \times 4 \text{ ft}$ bed has a height of $3 \text{ ft}$. A mosquito enters the net through a hole located at one of the bed's corners. It then flies to and settles at the upper corner of the net that is diagonally opposite. Assuming the hole is the origin, the bed's length lies along the X-axis, its width along the Y-axis, and the vertically upward direction is the Z-axis, determine the components of the displacement vector.
303401.sol:
The origin is taken at the hole where the mosquito enters, so the initial position vector is $\vec{r}_1 = 0\hat{i} + 0\hat{j} + 0\hat{k}$.

The mosquito flies to the diagonally opposite upper corner of the net.

The length of the bed is along the X-axis, so the x-component of the displacement is $7 \text{ ft}$.

The width of the bed is along the Y-axis, so the y-component of the displacement is $4 \text{ ft}$.

The vertically upward direction is along the Z-axis, so the z-component of the displacement is $3 \text{ ft}$.

The final position vector of the mosquito is $\vec{r}_2 = 7\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$.

The displacement vector is $\Delta\vec{r} = \vec{r}_2 - \vec{r}_1 = 7\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$.

The components of the displacement vector are $7 \text{ ft}, 4 \text{ ft}, 3 \text{ ft}$.

303533.text: When passing through an equilateral transparent prism, the minimum deviations experienced by red, yellow, and violet beams are $38.4^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$, $38.7^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$, and $39.2^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$ respectively. Determine the dispersive power of the medium.
303533.sol:
The dispersive power $\omega$ of a prism is defined as the ratio of angular dispersion to the mean deviation.

Angular dispersion is given by the difference in deviation of the extreme colours:

$\theta = \delta_v - \delta_r$

Mean deviation is given by the deviation of the yellow light:

$\delta = \delta_y$

Therefore, the dispersive power is:

$\omega = \dfrac{\delta_v - \delta_r}{\delta_y}$

Substituting the given values:

$\omega = \dfrac{39.2^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}} - 38.4^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}}}{38.7^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}}}$

$\omega = \dfrac{0.8^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}}}{38.7^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}}}$

$\omega \approx 0.0206$

304585.text: For a particle executing simple harmonic motion, the time period equals the duration between its consecutive appearances at a certain point during its motion. This point is
options: a point between the mean position and the negative extreme
a point between the mean position and the positive extreme
304585.sol:
Let the time period of the simple harmonic motion be $T$.

At the mean position, the particle crosses the point twice in one complete oscillation. The time interval between consecutive appearances is $\dfrac{T}{2}$.

At any point between the mean position and an extreme position, the particle crosses the point twice in one complete oscillation, while moving in opposite directions. The time intervals between consecutive appearances alternate between $t$ and $T-t$, neither of which is equal to $T$.

At an extreme position, the particle reaches the point only once in one complete oscillation. The time interval between consecutive appearances is exactly equal to the time period $T$.

304866.text: A screen is located at a distance of $40 \text{ cm}$ from an illuminated object. A converging lens is placed between the object and the screen in an attempt to form an image of the object on the screen. If no such position can be found, the focal length of the lens
options: must not be less than $10 \text{ cm}$
must not be greater than $20 \text{ cm}$
304866.sol:
Let the distance between the object and the screen be $D$, and the object distance from the lens be $x$.

The image distance from the lens is $D - x$.

Using the lens formula, $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$

$\dfrac{1}{D-x} - \dfrac{1}{-x} = \dfrac{1}{f}$

$\dfrac{x + D - x}{x(D-x)} = \dfrac{1}{f}$

$x^2 - Dx + Df = 0$

For a real position of the lens to exist, the roots of this quadratic equation must be real, which requires the discriminant to be greater than or equal to zero:

$D^2 - 4Df \ge 0 \Rightarrow D \ge 4f$

Since no such position can be found, the roots must be imaginary, which means:

$D < 4f$

Given $D = 40 \text{ cm}$, we have:

$40 < 4f \Rightarrow f > 10 \text{ cm}$

Therefore, the focal length of the lens must be greater than $10 \text{ cm}$.

305338.text: For a 6F6 triode tube, the plate current, plate voltage, and grid voltage are related by $i_p = 41(V_p + 7 V_g)^{1.41}$, where $V_p$ and $V_g$ are in volts and $i_p$ is in microamperes. If the tube is operated at $V_p = 250 \text{ V}$ and $V_g = -20 \text{ V}$, calculate the amplification factor.
305338.sol:
The plate current of a triode is generally expressed as $i_p = K(V_p + \mu V_g)^n$, where $\mu$ is the amplification factor.

Comparing the given equation $i_p = 41(V_p + 7 V_g)^{1.41}$ with the standard equation, we directly get $\mu = 7$.

Alternatively, the amplification factor is defined as $\mu = -\left(\dfrac{\partial V_p}{\partial V_g}\right)_{i_p}$.

For a constant $i_p$, differentiating the given equation yields:

$0 = 41 \times 1.41 (V_p + 7 V_g)^{0.41} (dV_p + 7 dV_g)$

$dV_p + 7 dV_g = 0$

$\mu = -\dfrac{dV_p}{dV_g} = 7$

305501.text: As shown in the figure, a long U-shaped wire of width $l$ is situated in a perpendicular magnetic field $B$. A wire of length $l$ is slid along the U-shaped wire towards the right at a constant velocity $v$. All wires possess a resistance of $r$ per unit length. At $t = 0$, the sliding wire is located near the left edge of the U-shaped wire. Determine the current flowing in the circuit at time $t$.
305501.sol:
The motional EMF induced in the sliding wire moving with velocity $v$ in a perpendicular magnetic field $B$ is given by:

$E = Blv$

At time $t$, the distance moved by the sliding wire is $x = vt$. The circuit forms a rectangular loop. The total length of the wire forming this loop consists of the left edge of the U-shaped wire (length $l$), the sliding wire (length $l$), and the top and bottom horizontal segments (each of length $vt$).

The total length of the conducting loop at time $t$ is:

$L = l + l + vt + vt = 2(l + vt)$

Since all wires have a resistance of $r$ per unit length, the total resistance of the circuit at time $t$ is:

$R = Lr = 2r(l + vt)$

The induced current $I$ in the circuit is:

$I = \dfrac{E}{R} = \dfrac{Blv}{2r(l + vt)}$

305608.text: Consider a very rough model of a beryllium atom. The nucleus consists of four protons and four neutrons, confined to a small volume of radius $10^{-15} \text{ m}$. The two $1s$ electrons form a spherical charge cloud at an average distance of $1.3 \times 10^{-11} \text{ m}$ from the nucleus, while the two $2s$ electrons form another spherical cloud at an average distance of $5.2 \times 10^{-11} \text{ m}$ from the nucleus. Determine the electric field at a point just inside the $1s$ cloud.
305608.sol:
By Gauss's law, the electric field at a distance $r$ from the center of a spherically symmetric charge distribution depends only on the net charge enclosed within a sphere of radius $r$.

For a point just inside the $1s$ cloud, the distance from the nucleus is $r = 1.3 \times 10^{-11} \text{ m}$. Since the point is just inside the electron cloud, the sphere of radius $r$ encloses only the nucleus. The electron clouds are outside this radius and do not contribute to the enclosed charge.

The beryllium nucleus contains $4$ protons, so the enclosed charge is $q = +4e = 4 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C} = 6.4 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.

The electric field is given by:

$E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q}{r^2}$

Substituting the given values:

$E = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 6.4 \times 10^{-19}}{(1.3 \times 10^{-11})^2}$

$E = \dfrac{57.6 \times 10^{-10}}{1.69 \times 10^{-22}}$

$E \approx 34.1 \times 10^{12} \text{ N C}^{-1} = 3.4 \times 10^{13} \text{ N C}^{-1}$

305802.text: On a given day, the temperature and humidity of air are $27^{}^{{}^{\circ}} \text{C}$ and $50\%$. Determine the amount of vapour that must be added to $1$ cubic metre of air to saturate it. The saturation vapour pressure at $27^{}^{{}^{\circ}} \text{C}$ is $3600 \text{ Pa}$.
305802.sol:
Relative humidity is given as $50\%$.

Initial vapour pressure $P_{1} = 0.50 \times 3600 = 1800 \text{ Pa}$.

To saturate the air, the vapour pressure must reach the saturation vapour pressure $P_{s} = 3600 \text{ Pa}$.

Additional vapour pressure required is $\Delta P = 3600 - 1800 = 1800 \text{ Pa}$.

Using the ideal gas equation, $\Delta P V = \dfrac{\Delta m}{M} R T$, where $V = 1 \text{ m}^{3}$, $T = 300 \text{ K}$, and $M = 18 \text{ g/mol}$ is the molar mass of water.

$\Delta m = \dfrac{\Delta P V M}{R T}$

$\Delta m = \dfrac{1800 \times 1 \times 18}{8.314 \times 300} \text{ g}$

$\Delta m = \dfrac{108}{8.314} \approx 13 \text{ g}$

305871.text: A circular wire-loop of radius $a$, carrying a current $i$, is placed in a perpendicular magnetic field $B$. Determine the force of compression in the wire.
305871.sol:
Consider a small element of the circular wire subtending an angle $d\theta$ at the center.

The length of this element is $dl = a d\theta$.

The magnetic force on this element is $dF = i(dl)B = i(a d\theta)B$.

By the right-hand rule for $d\vec{l} \times \vec{B}$, this force is directed radially inwards, causing a compressive force $T$ in the wire.

The compressive forces act tangentially at the ends of the small element. The radial component of these forces balances the inward magnetic force.

The net inward radial force due to compression is $2T \sin\left(\dfrac{d\theta}{2}\right)$.

For a small angle $d\theta$, $\sin\left(\dfrac{d\theta}{2}\right) \approx \dfrac{d\theta}{2}$.

Equating the forces for equilibrium:

$2T \left(\dfrac{d\theta}{2}\right) = i a B d\theta$

$T d\theta = i a B d\theta$

$T = i a B$

Alternatively, considering a semicircular portion of the wire, the total magnetic force is $F = i(2a)B = 2iaB$ directed towards the center. This is balanced by the compressive forces at the two ends, so $2T = 2iaB \Rightarrow T = iaB$.

305906.text: Consider two particles, each of mass $m$, positioned at a separation distance $d$ inside a uniform magnetic field $B$. The particles possess opposite charges of equal magnitude $q$. At an initial time $t = 0$, they are projected directly towards one another, each travelling with a speed $v$. Assume that the Coulomb interaction between the charges is turned off. Let $v_m$ denote the maximum projection speed that allows the particles to avoid a collision. Suppose the particles are projected with a speed $v = 2 v_m$ and undergo a completely inelastic collision. How will the combined mass move following the collision?
options: It moves with a constant speed $2 v_m$ along a straight line drawn upward in the plane of the figure through the point of collision.
It moves in a circular path of radius $d$ with a constant speed $v_m$.
It moves with a constant speed $v_m$ along a straight line drawn upward in the plane of the figure through the point of collision.
It comes to rest immediately at the point of collision.
305906.sol:
The magnetic force on a moving charge is given by $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$. For the particle with charge $q$ moving with velocity $v\hat{i}$ in a magnetic field $-B\hat{k}$, the force is $qvB\hat{j}$ (upwards). For the particle with charge $-q$ moving with velocity $-v\hat{i}$, the force is also $qvB\hat{j}$ (upwards). Thus, both particles move in circular paths curving upwards.

The radius of the circular path is $R = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$.

To just avoid collision, the two circular paths must be tangent to each other. Since the initial separation is $d$, the sum of their radii must be equal to $d$.

$2R_m = d \Rightarrow R_m = \dfrac{d}{2}$

The maximum speed to avoid collision is $v_m = \dfrac{qBR_m}{m} = \dfrac{qBd}{2m}$.

When the particles are projected with speed $v = 2v_m$, the new radius of their paths is $R = \dfrac{m(2v_m)}{qB} = 2R_m = d$.

Let the collision occur after the velocity vectors have rotated by an angle $\theta$. The horizontal distance covered by each particle is $\dfrac{d}{2}$.

From the geometry of the circular path, the horizontal displacement is $R \sin\theta$.

$R \sin\theta = \dfrac{d}{2}$

Substituting $R = d$, we get $\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \theta = 30^{\circ}$.

The velocities of the particles just before the collision are:

$\vec{v}_1 = v \cos(30^{\circ})\hat{i} + v \sin(30^{\circ})\hat{j}$

$\vec{v}_2 = -v \cos(30^{\circ})\hat{i} + v \sin(30^{\circ})\hat{j}$

Since the collision is completely inelastic, the particles stick together. By conservation of linear momentum:

$m\vec{v}_1 + m\vec{v}_2 = (2m)\vec{v}_f$

$\vec{v}_f = \dfrac{\vec{v}_1 + \vec{v}_2}{2} = v \sin(30^{\circ})\hat{j} = \dfrac{v}{2}\hat{j}$

Given $v = 2v_m$, the final velocity is $\vec{v}_f = v_m\hat{j}$.

The combined mass has a net charge of $q + (-q) = 0$. Therefore, it experiences no magnetic force and moves with a constant speed $v_m$ along a straight line drawn upward.

Answer: It moves with a constant speed $v_m$ along a straight line drawn upward in the plane of the figure through the point of collision.

306753.subject: Physics
306753.text: For the molecules of an ideal gas in equilibrium, which of the following quantities has an average value of zero?
306753.sol:
For an ideal gas in thermal equilibrium, the molecules are in continuous random motion in all possible directions.

Since velocity is a vector quantity and all directions of motion are equally probable, the average velocity of the gas molecules is zero ($\langle \vec{v} \rangle = 0$).

Momentum is the product of mass and velocity ($\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$). Since the average velocity is zero, the average momentum of the gas molecules is also zero.

Speed, density, and kinetic energy are scalar quantities and are strictly positive for a gas in equilibrium, so their average values are non-zero.

306826.subject: Physics
306826.text: In a lithium vapour at room temperature, two lithium nuclei do not combine to form a carbon nucleus because
options: Coulomb repulsion prevents the nuclei from coming very close
a carbon nucleus is an unstable particle
a lithium nucleus is bound more tightly than a carbon nucleus
the process is not energetically favourable
306826.sol:
At room temperature, the thermal kinetic energy of lithium nuclei is very small (of the order of $kT$).

For two lithium nuclei to fuse and form a carbon nucleus, they must approach each other within the range of the strong nuclear force (approximately $10^{-15}$ m).

Since both lithium nuclei are positively charged, they experience a strong electrostatic (Coulomb) repulsion.

The kinetic energy at room temperature is completely insufficient to overcome this Coulomb barrier, preventing the nuclei from coming close enough to fuse.

The following text is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the text:

Rapid urbanisation has converted fertile agriculture, forests and wetlands into concreted areas that are unable to retain rainwater or channel them into tributary streams that feed the Cauvery. Urbanisation demands concrete; concrete requires sand. In the districts sur-rounding the Cauvery, rampant sand mining has altered the natural topography of the river, eroding its banks, widening the river and altering water flow patterns. Despite warnings from environmentalist groups and farmer coalitions, and interventions by the court, this practice continues unchecked. It is no surprise that the wells that replenish farms across the basin are running dry-or that desperate farmers are reduced to abandoning agriculture and renting their farms to sand contractors for sand storage, thus becoming complicit in their own destruction.
options: In order to meet the huge demand for sand caused by rapid urbanisation, sand mining is taking place unrestrained in the districts surrounding the Cauvery, despite resistance from environmentalist groups and farmer coalitions with the result, the wells that replenish farms across the Cauvery basin are running dry.

Rapid urbanisation has placed a huge demand on construction material like sand, and in order to meet this demand rampant sand mining is taking place in fertile regions surrounding the Cauvery basin and farmers in this region are renting out their farms to sand contractors as they find it more lucrative than agriculture.

To meet the huge demand on sand due to rapid urbanisation, rampant sand mining is done in the districts surrounding the Cauvery, despite resistance from environmentalists and farmer coalitions, and hence the wet is that replenish farms are running dry, forcing farmers to abandon agriculture and rent their farms to sand contractors, thus conniving in their destruction.

Rapid urbanisation in the areas surrounding the Cauvery basin has led to a huge demand for sand hence farmers in the region, in connivance with sand contractors, are involved in rampant sand mining, thus being a cause for their destruction.
306968.sol:
The following are the main points of the paragraph: (1) Rampant sand mining is taking place in the districts surrounding the Cauvery despite resistance from environmentalists, etc. (2) With the wells running dry due to sand mining farmers are forced to rent their farms to sand contractors, thereby bringing their own destruction. Choice (a): This cannot be the best summary because it fails to mention the second point. Choice (b ): This option, which states that farmers find sand mining more lucrative, is a distortion of the original as this point is not mentioned in the paragraph. Choice (c): Correct. This option summarises the paragraph most appropriately. Choice (d): This option, which states that farmers connive with the sand contractors, is also a distortion.

Hence, option (c) best summarises the passage.

The given reactant is $N,N$-dimethylaniline, which is a tertiary aromatic amine.

The reagent mixture of $\text{NaNO}_2$ and $\text{HCl}$ generates nitrous acid ($\text{HNO}_2$), which produces the nitrosonium ion ($\text{NO}^+$) as an electrophile.

Tertiary aromatic amines undergo electrophilic aromatic substitution when treated with nitrous acid. The $-\text{N(CH}_3)_2$ group is strongly ring-activating and directs the incoming electrophile to the ortho and para positions.

Due to significant steric hindrance at the ortho position, the electrophile ($\text{NO}^+$) attacks the para position predominantly.

309530.subject: Chemistry
309530.text: Which of the following compounds has the highest boiling point?
309530.sol:
The boiling point of a compound depends on the strength of its intermolecular forces.

$\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{CO}_{2}\mathrm{H}$ (acetic acid) has an $-\mathrm{OH}$ group and a $\mathrm{C=O}$ group, allowing it to form strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds. It exists as a dimer in the liquid phase, which significantly increases its boiling point.

$\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{CH}_{2}\mathrm{OH}$ (ethanol) also exhibits intermolecular hydrogen bonding, but the extent and strength of hydrogen bonding are lesser than in acetic acid.

$\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COCH}_{3}$ (acetone) has dipole-dipole interactions but lacks the ability to form intermolecular hydrogen bonds with itself.

$\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{OCH}_{3}$ (dimethyl ether) has only weak dipole-dipole interactions and van der Waals forces.

Due to the strongest intermolecular hydrogen bonding, $\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{CO}_{2}\mathrm{H}$ has the highest boiling point among the given compounds.

Answer: $\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{CO}_{2}\mathrm{H}$

313325.subject: IOQM
313325.text: A pen costs $₹ 11$ and a notebook costs $₹ 13$. Find the number of ways in which a person can spend exactly ₹ 1000 to buy pens and notebooks.
313325.sol:
Cost of a pen is $₹ 11$
Cost of a notebook is ₹ 13
$\begin{aligned}
& 11 x+13 y=1000 \\
& y=\frac{1000-11 x}{13} \in I \\
& \frac{12-11 x}{13} \in I \Rightarrow \frac{(13-1)-(13 x-2 x)}{13} \in I \\
& \frac{2 x-1}{13} \in I \Rightarrow \frac{12 x-6}{13} \in I \\
& \frac{13 x-(x+6)}{13} \in I \Rightarrow \frac{x+6}{13} \in I \\
& x=13 \lambda-6 \quad(1 \leq x \leq 90) \\
& x \in\{7,20, \ldots \ldots, 85\} \quad\{\lambda=\{1,2, \ldots, 3\}\}
\end{aligned}$

6a104ff98b46719ce7976cfc.subject: Chemistry
6a104ff98b46719ce7976cfc.text:
Observe the given structure of 1-buten-3-yne where specific bonds are labeled as 'a', 'b', 'c', and 'd'. Match the labeled bonds in List I with their corresponding nature in List II.

List IList II
ABond 'a'IOne $\sigma$ and two $\pi$ bonds
BBond 'b'IIOne $\sigma$ bond formed by $sp^2-sp$ overlap
CBond 'c'IIIOne $\sigma$ and one $\pi$ bond
DBond 'd'IVOne $\sigma$ bond formed by $sp-s$ overlap

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
6a104ff98b46719ce7976cfc.sol:
The given molecule is 1-buten-3-yne: $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{C}\equiv\text{C}-\text{H}$.

First, determine the hybridization of each carbon atom:
The terminal carbon $C_1$ ($\text{CH}_2=$) is bonded to three atoms with no lone pairs, so it is $sp^2$ hybridized.
The carbon $C_2$ ($=\text{CH}-$) is bonded to three atoms, so it is $sp^2$ hybridized.
The carbon $C_3$ ($-\text{C}\equiv$) is bonded to two atoms, so it is $sp$ hybridized.
The carbon $C_4$ ($\equiv\text{C}-\text{H}$) is bonded to two atoms, so it is $sp$ hybridized.

Now, analyze the labeled bonds:
Bond 'a' is a double bond between $C_1$ and $C_2$. A double bond consists of one $\sigma$ bond and one $\pi$ bond. (A $\rightarrow$ III)
Bond 'b' is a single bond between $C_2$ ($sp^2$) and $C_3$ ($sp$). It is a $\sigma$ bond formed by the overlap of an $sp^2$ orbital and an $sp$ orbital. (B $\rightarrow$ II)
Bond 'c' is a triple bond between $C_3$ and $C_4$. A triple bond consists of one $\sigma$ bond and two $\pi$ bonds. (C $\rightarrow$ I)
Bond 'd' is a single bond between $C_4$ ($sp$) and a hydrogen atom ($s$). It is a $\sigma$ bond formed by the overlap of an $sp$ orbital and an $s$ orbital. (D $\rightarrow$ IV)

Therefore, the correct matching is A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV.

Answer: A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV

6a16f3267cfacf7984f866db.subject: Physics
6a16f3267cfacf7984f866db.text: In the circuit shown below, $D_1$ and $D_2$ are silicon diodes. Assuming the knee voltage (barrier potential) of a silicon diode to be $0.7\text{ V}$, what is the current supplied by the battery?
6a16f3267cfacf7984f866db.sol:
The positive terminal of the battery is connected to the p-side of diode $D_1$ and the n-side of diode $D_2$.

Therefore, $D_1$ is forward-biased and $D_2$ is reverse-biased.

The branch containing $D_2$ acts as an open circuit, so no current flows through $R_3$.

The active circuit is a series loop with the battery, $R_1$, $D_1$, and $R_2$.

The net voltage driving the current is the battery voltage minus the barrier potential of the forward-biased diode $D_1$.

$V_{net} = 3.7 - 0.7 = 3.0$ V

The equivalent resistance of the active circuit is the sum of the series resistors $R_1$ and $R_2$.

$R_{eq} = R_1 + R_2 = 5 + 5 = 10\ \Omega$

The current supplied by the battery is calculated using Ohm's law.

$I = \dfrac{V_{net}}{R_{eq}} = \dfrac{3.0}{10} = 0.30$ A

Answer: $0.30\text{ A}$

6a16f3267cfacf7984f866e1.text:
Given below is an outline of the modern periodic table where four elements are marked as P, Q, R, and S.

Match List I (the marked elements) with List II (their characteristic properties) based on their positions in the periodic groups.

List IList II
AElement PIHighest negative electron gain enthalpy
BElement QIIMost electronegative element
CElement RIIILowest ionization enthalpy
DElement SIVHighest ionization enthalpy

Identify the correct answer from the options given below:
6a16f3267cfacf7984f866e1.sol:
Based on the given outline of the modern periodic table, the elements are identified as follows:

Element P is in Group 1 and Period 6, which corresponds to Cesium (Cs). Cesium has the largest atomic size among stable elements and consequently the lowest ionization enthalpy. Thus, A matches with III.

Element Q is in Group 17 and Period 2, which corresponds to Fluorine (F). Fluorine is the most electronegative element in the periodic table. Thus, B matches with II.

Element R is in Group 17 and Period 3, which corresponds to Chlorine (Cl). Chlorine has the highest negative electron gain enthalpy due to its relatively smaller size and higher effective nuclear charge compared to other halogens, but larger size than fluorine which reduces interelectronic repulsions. Thus, C matches with I.

Element S is in Group 18 and Period 1, which corresponds to Helium (He). Helium has a completely filled $1s^2$ shell and the smallest atomic size among noble gases, giving it the highest ionization enthalpy of all elements. Thus, D matches with IV.

The correct matching is A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV.

Answer: A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV

6a2109ad219e1ae5a1722914.text: If $\eta$ and $\rho$ respectively denote the coefficient of viscosity and the density of a liquid, then the ratio $\dfrac{\eta}{\rho}$ has the dimensions of:
6a2109ad219e1ae5a1722914.sol:
The dimensional formula for the coefficient of viscosity $\eta$ is given by:

$\eta = \dfrac{F}{A \left(\dfrac{dv}{dx}\right)}$

$[\eta] = \dfrac{[M L T^{-2}]}{[L^2] [T^{-1}]} = [M L^{-1} T^{-1}]$

The dimensional formula for density $\rho$ is:

$[\rho] = \dfrac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Volume}} = [M L^{-3}]$

The ratio of the coefficient of viscosity to density is:

$\dfrac{[\eta]}{[\rho]} = \dfrac{[M L^{-1} T^{-1}]}{[M L^{-3}]} = [M^0 L^2 T^{-1}]$

Answer: $[M^0 L^2 T^{-1}]$

6a2109ae219e1ae5a172292a.subject: Physics
6a2109ae219e1ae5a172292a.text: Two isolated point masses $2M$ and $5M$ are initially at rest in free space. They start moving towards each other strictly under mutual gravitational attraction. At a certain instant, if the mass $2M$ has moved a distance $y$, what is the distance covered by the mass $5M$ at that same instant?
6a2109ae219e1ae5a172292a.sol:
Since no external force acts on the system of the two masses, the center of mass of the system remains at rest.

Let the distance moved by the mass $2M$ be $d_1$ and the distance moved by the mass $5M$ be $d_2$.

From the conservation of the position of the center of mass:

$m_1 d_1 = m_2 d_2$

Substituting the given values $m_1 = 2M$, $m_2 = 5M$, and $d_1 = y$:

$2M y = 5M d_2$

$d_2 = \dfrac{2y}{5}$

The distance covered by the mass $5M$ is $\dfrac{2y}{5}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{2y}{5}$

6a2a77bcfad2360f42564b8d.subject: Physics
6a2a77bcfad2360f42564b8d.text:
Five identical coins are dropped from rest from different balconies of a tall building. The time taken by each coin to reach the ground is recorded as follows (neglecting air resistance):
A. Coin A takes $3.0$ s.
B. Coin B takes $1.5$ s.
C. Coin C takes $2.5$ s.
D. Coin D takes $4.0$ s.
E. Coin E takes $2.0$ s.
What is the correct order of the heights of the balconies from which the coins were dropped?
6a2a77bcfad2360f42564b8d.sol:
For an object dropped from rest, the height $h$ is given by $h = \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2$.

Since $g$ is constant, $h \propto t^2$. Thus, the height of the balcony is directly proportional to the square of the time taken to reach the ground. A longer time corresponds to a greater height.

The given times are:
$t_D = 4.0$ s
$t_A = 3.0$ s
$t_C = 2.5$ s
$t_E = 2.0$ s
$t_B = 1.5$ s

Arranging the times in descending order gives $t_D > t_A > t_C > t_E > t_B$.

Therefore, the correct order of the heights is $D > A > C > E > B$.

Answer: $D > A > C > E > B$

6a0e2779165ae1327797b3ca.text:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the classification of enzymes:

List-IList-II
(A)Ligases(I)Catalyse removal of groups from substrates by mechanisms other than hydrolysis leaving double bonds
(B)Lyases(II)Catalyse the linking together of two compounds
(C)Hydrolases(III)Catalyse inter-conversion of optical, geometric or positional isomers
(D)Isomerases(IV)Catalyse hydrolysis of ester, ether, peptide or glycosidic bonds

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
6a0e2779165ae1327797b3ca.sol:
Ligases are enzymes that catalyse the linking together of two compounds, such as joining of C-O, C-S, C-N, P-O etc. bonds. Thus, (A) matches with (II).

Lyases are enzymes that catalyse the removal of groups from substrates by mechanisms other than hydrolysis, leaving double bonds. Thus, (B) matches with (I).

Hydrolases are enzymes that catalyse the hydrolysis of ester, ether, peptide, glycosidic, C-C, C-halide or P-N bonds. Thus, (C) matches with (IV).

Isomerases are enzymes that catalyse the inter-conversion of optical, geometric or positional isomers. Thus, (D) matches with (III).

The correct matching is (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III).

Answer: (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)

6a16f3287cfacf7984f86730.subject: Biology
6a16f3287cfacf7984f86730.text:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: When a new habitat is just being colonized, natality contributes more significantly to population growth than immigration.
Statement II: The population density of a given habitat will decrease if the sum of mortality and emigration exceeds the sum of natality and immigration.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
6a16f3287cfacf7984f86730.sol:
Statement I is incorrect because when a new habitat is just being colonized, immigration contributes more significantly to population growth than natality (birth rates).

Statement II is correct because the population density at time $t+1$ is given by the equation $N_{t+1} = N_t + [(B + I) - (D + E)]$, where $B$ is natality, $I$ is immigration, $D$ is mortality, and $E$ is emigration. If the sum of mortality and emigration $(D + E)$ exceeds the sum of natality and immigration $(B + I)$, the term in the bracket becomes negative, and the population density will decrease.

Answer: Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

Match List I with List II :

List IList II
AGlucocorticoids1Increases heart beat and strength of heart contraction

6a2a77c0fad2360f42564bfb.sol:
Glucocorticoids stimulate gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, and proteolysis, and inhibit cellular uptake and utilization of amino acids.

Androgenic steroids secreted by the adrenal cortex play a role in the growth of axial hair, pubic hair, and facial hair during puberty.

Catecholamines (adrenaline and noradrenaline) increase the heart beat, the strength of heart contraction, and the rate of respiration.

Erythropoietin is a peptide hormone produced by the juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney which stimulates erythropoiesis (formation of red blood cells).

Therefore, the correct matching is A-3, B-4, C-1, D-2.

Answer: A-3, B-4, C-1, D-2

6a7a1ff884b172edc8240d0d.subject: Physics
6a7a1ff884b172edc8240d0d.text: Two infinitely large parallel conducting plates A and B are separated by a distance $d$. They have uniform surface charge densities of $+4\sigma$ and $-2\sigma$ respectively. A point charge $+q$ of mass $m$ is released from rest at the surface of Plate A. The kinetic energy of the charge $+q$ just before it reaches Plate B is :
6a7a1ff884b172edc8240d0d.sol:
The net electric field in the region between the plates is the vector sum of the fields due to Plate A and Plate B.

Since Plate A has a positive charge density and Plate B has a negative charge density, both fields point in the same direction (from A to B).

Magnitude of the net electric field $E$ is:
$E = \dfrac{\sigma_A}{2\epsilon_0} - \dfrac{\sigma_B}{2\epsilon_0} = \dfrac{4\sigma}{2\epsilon_0} - \dfrac{(-2\sigma)}{2\epsilon_0}$

$E = \dfrac{4\sigma + 2\sigma}{2\epsilon_0} = \dfrac{6\sigma}{2\epsilon_0} = \dfrac{3\sigma}{\epsilon_0}$

The force experienced by the charge $+q$ is:
$F = qE = \dfrac{3\sigma q}{\epsilon_0}$

The work done by the electric field as the charge moves a distance $d$ from Plate A to Plate B is:
$W = Fd = \dfrac{3\sigma q d}{\epsilon_0}$

According to the work-energy theorem, the kinetic energy of the charge just before reaching Plate B is equal to the work done by the electric field:
$K = W = \dfrac{3\sigma q d}{\epsilon_0}$

Answer: $\dfrac{3\sigma q d}{\epsilon_0}$

6a7a1ff82a22c17b4e91cda1.subject: Physics
6a7a1ff82a22c17b4e91cda1.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
6a7a1ff82a22c17b4e91cda1.text:
Block $A$ of mass $1\text{ kg}$ is released from rest from a height of $1.8\text{ m}$ on a smooth curved track. At the bottom of the track, it collides perfectly elastically with Block $B$ of mass $2\text{ kg}$, which is initially at rest. After the collision, Block $B$ slides along a smooth horizontal surface and compresses a horizontal ideal spring of spring constant $8\text{ N m}^{-1}$. The maximum compression in the spring is :
(Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
6a7a1ff82a22c17b4e91cda1.sol:
By conservation of mechanical energy, the velocity of Block $A$ just before the collision is:
$v_1 = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2 \times 10 \times 1.8} = 6\text{ m s}^{-1}$

For a perfectly elastic collision, the velocity of Block $B$ just after the collision is given by:
$v_2' = \left(\dfrac{2m_1}{m_1 + m_2}\right) v_1$
$v_2' = \left(\dfrac{2 \times 1}{1 + 2}\right) \times 6 = 4\text{ m s}^{-1}$

Applying conservation of mechanical energy for Block $B$ and the spring:
$\dfrac{1}{2} m_2 (v_2')^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} k x^2$
$\dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times (4)^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 8 \times x^2$
$16 = 4x^2 \Rightarrow x = 2\text{ m}$

Answer: $2\text{ m}$

6a7a1ff893a945e639aa37b6.text: Two satellites $A$ and $B$ are revolving in circular orbits around a planet. The orbital speed of satellite $A$ is twice the orbital speed of satellite $B$. If the time period of satellite $A$ is $T$, then the time period of satellite $B$ will be
6a7a1ff893a945e639aa37b6.sol:
The orbital speed of a satellite is given by $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{R}}$, which implies $R \propto \dfrac{1}{v^2}$.

According to Kepler's Third Law, the time period $T$ is related to the orbital radius $R$ by $T^2 \propto R^3$.

Substituting the proportionality for $R$ into Kepler's law:
$T^2 \propto \left(\dfrac{1}{v^2}\right)^3$
$T^2 \propto \dfrac{1}{v^6}$
$T \propto \dfrac{1}{v^3}$

We are given that $v_A = 2v_B$, and $T_A = T$.

Taking the ratio of the time periods of $B$ and $A$:
$\dfrac{T_B}{T_A} = \left(\dfrac{v_A}{v_B}\right)^3$

$\dfrac{T_B}{T} = (2)^3 = 8$

$T_B = 8T$

Answer: $8T$

6a7a1ff87e075c6b0bf787a9.subject: Physics
6a7a1ff87e075c6b0bf787a9.text: A liquid having a heat capacity of $1800 \text{ J K}^{-1}$ cools from $80^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $60^{\circ}\text{C}$ in $12$ minutes. The temperature of the surroundings is $20^{\circ}\text{C}$. An electrical heater is now immersed in the liquid to maintain its temperature at a steady $80^{\circ}\text{C}$. Assuming Newton's law of cooling is valid, the power of the heater required is ________ $\text{W}$.
6a7a1ff87e075c6b0bf787a9.sol:
Using the average temperature approximation of Newton's law of cooling for the first process:
$\dfrac{\Delta T}{\Delta t} = K\left(\dfrac{T_1 + T_2}{2} - T_0\right)$

The liquid cools from $80^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $60^{\circ}\text{C}$ in $12$ minutes:
$\dfrac{80 - 60}{12} = K\left(\dfrac{80 + 60}{2} - 20\right)$
$\Rightarrow \dfrac{20}{12} = K(70 - 20)$
$\Rightarrow \dfrac{5}{3} = K(50)$
$\Rightarrow K = \dfrac{1}{30} \text{ min}^{-1}$

To maintain the liquid at a steady temperature of $80^{\circ}\text{C}$, the heater must supply heat at the same rate the liquid loses heat to the surroundings at $80^{\circ}\text{C}$.
The rate of cooling at $80^{\circ}\text{C}$ is:
$\dfrac{dT}{dt} = K(T - T_0) = \dfrac{1}{30}(80 - 20) = \dfrac{60}{30} = 2^{\circ}\text{C min}^{-1}$

The rate of heat loss is:
$\dfrac{dQ}{dt} = C \dfrac{dT}{dt} = 1800 \times 2 = 3600 \text{ J min}^{-1}$

Converting this to Watts (Joules per second):
$P = \dfrac{3600 \text{ J}}{60 \text{ s}} = 60 \text{ W}$

Answer: $60$

6a7a1ff817d8d7b437324fab.subject: Physics
6a7a1ff817d8d7b437324fab.text: A parallel plate capacitor of capacitance $C_0$ is charged to a potential difference $V_0$ by a battery. The battery is then disconnected. A dielectric slab of thickness equal to half the plate separation and dielectric constant $K=3$ is inserted between the plates. The final electrostatic energy stored in the capacitor is :
6a7a1ff817d8d7b437324fab.sol:
Since the battery is disconnected, the charge on the capacitor remains constant.
Initial charge, $Q = C_0 V_0$

Let the plate separation be $d$. The initial capacitance is $C_0 = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}$.
When a dielectric slab of thickness $t = \dfrac{d}{2}$ and $K=3$ is inserted, the new capacitance $C_f$ is:
$C_f = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d - t + \dfrac{t}{K}} = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d - \dfrac{d}{2} + \dfrac{d}{2 \times 3}}$
$C_f = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 A}{\dfrac{d}{2} + \dfrac{d}{6}} = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 A}{\dfrac{4d}{6}} = \dfrac{3}{2} \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d} = \dfrac{3}{2} C_0$

The final electrostatic energy stored in the capacitor is:
$U_f = \dfrac{Q^2}{2 C_f} = \dfrac{(C_0 V_0)^2}{2 \left(\dfrac{3}{2} C_0\right)} = \dfrac{C_0^2 V_0^2}{3 C_0} = \dfrac{1}{3} C_0 V_0^2$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{3} C_0 V_0^2$

6a7a1ff818c67d713c70e2e5.subject: Physics
6a7a1ff818c67d713c70e2e5.text:
A particle of mass $2.21 \times 10^{-28} \mathrm{~kg}$ has a de Broglie wavelength exactly equal to the wavelength of an electromagnetic wave propagating in a vacuum with a frequency of $10^{14} \mathrm{~Hz}$. The velocity of the particle is
(Take $c = 3 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~m/s}$, $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{~J.s}$)
6a7a1ff818c67d713c70e2e5.sol:
The wavelength of the electromagnetic wave is given by:
$\lambda = \dfrac{c}{\nu} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^8}{10^{14}} = 3 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}$

The de Broglie wavelength of the particle is equal to this wavelength:
$\lambda_{\text{dB}} = \lambda = 3 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}$

Using the de Broglie relation $\lambda_{\text{dB}} = \dfrac{h}{mv}$, the velocity of the particle is:
$v = \dfrac{h}{m \lambda_{\text{dB}}}$

Substituting the given values:
$v = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{2.21 \times 10^{-28} \times 3 \times 10^{-6}}$

$v = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{6.63 \times 10^{-34}} = 1 \mathrm{~m/s}$

Answer: $1 \mathrm{~m/s}$

6a7a1ff8bf15f964e87c6bdc.subject: Physics
6a7a1ff8bf15f964e87c6bdc.text:
The digital input signals $A$ and $B$, and the output signal $Y$ of a logic circuit are observed over a time period from $t=0$ to $t=4$ seconds. The logic states (HIGH as 1, LOW as 0) change every second as follows:
From $t=0$ to $1$ s: $A = 0, B = 0$
From $t=1$ to $2$ s: $A = 0, B = 1$
From $t=2$ to $3$ s: $A = 1, B = 0$
From $t=3$ to $4$ s: $A = 1, B = 1$
The output $Y$ is observed to be HIGH only during the interval from $t=3$ to $4$ s, and LOW otherwise.

Which of the following logic circuits, constructed entirely using NOR gates, produces this output $Y$?
options: A single NOR gate with inputs $A$ and $B$.
A NOR gate with inputs $A$ and $B$, whose output is connected to both inputs of a second NOR gate.

Input $A$ is connected to both inputs of a first NOR gate, input $B$ is connected to both inputs of a second NOR gate, and the outputs of these two gates are connected to the inputs of a third NOR gate.
Input $A$ is connected to both inputs of a first NOR gate, and its output is connected along with input $B$ to the inputs of a second NOR gate.
6a7a1ff8bf15f964e87c6bdc.sol:
From the given time intervals, we can construct the truth table for the circuit:
When $A=0, B=0 \Rightarrow Y=0$
When $A=0, B=1 \Rightarrow Y=0$
When $A=1, B=0 \Rightarrow Y=0$
When $A=1, B=1 \Rightarrow Y=1$

This truth table corresponds to an AND gate ($Y = A \cdot B$).

Now, let us evaluate the given circuits constructed using NOR gates:
Option 1: A single NOR gate gives $Y = \overline{A+B}$.
Option 2: The first NOR gate gives $\overline{A+B}$. The second NOR gate acts as a NOT gate, giving $Y = \overline{\overline{A+B} + \overline{A+B}} = A+B$ (OR gate).
Option 3: The first two NOR gates act as NOT gates, producing $\overline{A}$ and $\overline{B}$. The third NOR gate takes these as inputs, giving $Y = \overline{\overline{A} + \overline{B}}$. By De Morgan's law, $Y = \overline{\overline{A}} \cdot \overline{\overline{B}} = A \cdot B$ (AND gate).
Option 4: The first NOR gate produces $\overline{A}$. The second NOR gate gives $Y = \overline{\overline{A} + B} = A \cdot \overline{B}$.

Therefore, the circuit in Option 3 produces the required output.

Answer: Input $A$ is connected to both inputs of a first NOR gate, input $B$ is connected to both inputs of a second NOR gate, and the outputs of these two gates are connected to the inputs of a third NOR gate.

6a7a1ff8a5584e4d42b6514f.subject: Chemistry
6a7a1ff8a5584e4d42b6514f.text:
A mixture containing $28\text{ g}$ of ethene ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$) and $48\text{ g}$ of oxygen gas is allowed to react in a closed vessel. The mass of carbon dioxide produced after the reaction is completed is :
(Given molar masses in $\text{g mol}^{-1}$ : $\text{C} = 12$, $\text{H} = 1$, $\text{O} = 16$)
6a7a1ff8a5584e4d42b6514f.sol:
The balanced chemical equation for the combustion of ethene is:
$\text{C}_2\text{H}_4(\text{g}) + 3\text{O}_2(\text{g}) \rightarrow 2\text{CO}_2(\text{g}) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l})$

Molar mass of $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 = 28\text{ g mol}^{-1}$
Moles of $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 = \dfrac{28}{28} = 1\text{ mol}$

Molar mass of $\text{O}_2 = 32\text{ g mol}^{-1}$
Moles of $\text{O}_2 = \dfrac{48}{32} = 1.5\text{ mol}$

From the stoichiometry, $1\text{ mol}$ of $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$ requires $3\text{ mol}$ of $\text{O}_2$.
Since only $1.5\text{ mol}$ of $\text{O}_2$ is available, $\text{O}_2$ is the limiting reagent.

According to the balanced equation, $3\text{ mol}$ of $\text{O}_2$ produces $2\text{ mol}$ of $\text{CO}_2$.
Therefore, $1.5\text{ mol}$ of $\text{O}_2$ will produce $\dfrac{2}{3} \times 1.5 = 1.0\text{ mol}$ of $\text{CO}_2$.

Molar mass of $\text{CO}_2 = 44\text{ g mol}^{-1}$
Mass of $\text{CO}_2 \text{ produced} = 1.0\text{ mol} \times 44\text{ g mol}^{-1} = 44\text{ g}$

Answer: 44

6a7a1ff861e6a495ef95289f.subject: Chemistry
6a7a1ff861e6a495ef95289f.text:
A $1\text{ L}$ buffer solution contains $0.3\text{ M}$ acetic acid and $0.3\text{ M}$ sodium acetate. A certain mass of solid $\text{NaOH}$ is added to the solution, which changes its $\text{pH}$ by $0.30$ units. Assuming no change in the volume of the solution, the mass of solid $\text{NaOH}$ added is:
(Given: $\text{pK}_{\text{a}}$ of acetic acid $= 4.74$, $\log 2 = 0.30$, Molar mass of $\text{NaOH} = 40\text{ g mol}^{-1}$)
6a7a1ff861e6a495ef95289f.sol:
Initial concentration of acetic acid $= 0.3\text{ M}$ and sodium acetate $= 0.3\text{ M}$.
Initial $\text{pH} = \text{pK}_{\text{a}} + \log \left( \dfrac{0.3}{0.3} \right) = 4.74$.

Addition of a strong base ($\text{NaOH}$) will increase the $\text{pH}$. Thus, the new $\text{pH}$ is:
$\text{pH}_{\text{new}} = 4.74 + 0.30 = 5.04$

Let $x$ be the number of moles of solid $\text{NaOH}$ added to $1\text{ L}$ of the buffer.
The added $\text{NaOH}$ reacts with acetic acid to form more sodium acetate.
New moles of salt $= 0.3 + x$
New moles of acid $= 0.3 - x$

Applying the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation:
$5.04 = 4.74 + \log \left( \dfrac{0.3 + x}{0.3 - x} \right)$

$0.30 = \log \left( \dfrac{0.3 + x}{0.3 - x} \right)$

Since $\log 2 = 0.30$, we have:
$\dfrac{0.3 + x}{0.3 - x} = 2$

$0.3 + x = 0.6 - 2x$
$3x = 0.3$
$x = 0.1\text{ mol}$

Mass of $\text{NaOH}$ added $= \text{moles} \times \text{molar mass} = 0.1 \times 40 = 4.0\text{ g}$.

Answer: $4.0\text{ g}$

6a7a1ff8c053ec1cb0eb794c.subject: Chemistry
6a7a1ff8c053ec1cb0eb794c.text: Which of the following sets of aromatic compounds completely fails to undergo Friedel-Crafts alkylation?
6a7a1ff8c053ec1cb0eb794c.sol:
Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation reactions do not occur on strongly deactivated benzene rings. Groups like $-\mathrm{NO_2}$, $-\mathrm{COOH}$, $-\mathrm{CHO}$, $-\mathrm{CN}$, and $-\mathrm{COR}$ are strong electron-withdrawing groups that decrease the electron density on the benzene ring to such an extent that the electrophile cannot attack it.

Furthermore, aniline has an $-\mathrm{NH_2}$ group which acts as a Lewis base. It reacts with the Lewis acid catalyst (like $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$) to form a strongly deactivated complex, thus preventing the Friedel-Crafts reaction.

Chlorobenzene, toluene, and anisole have groups that do not deactivate the ring strongly enough to prevent the reaction (halogens are weakly deactivating, while alkyl and alkoxy groups are activating).

Therefore, the set containing aniline, nitrobenzene, and benzoic acid completely fails to undergo Friedel-Crafts alkylation.

Answer: Aniline, nitrobenzene, benzoic acid

6a7a1ff8328f0296af624a6d.subject: Chemistry
6a7a1ff8328f0296af624a6d.text: Two aqueous solutions of urea (molar mass $= 60\text{ g/mol}$) are prepared. Solution I has a volume of $250\text{ mL}$ and a molarity of $0.4\text{ M}$. Solution II has a total mass of $106\text{ g}$. If both solutions contain the exact same mass of urea, what is the molality of Solution II?
6a7a1ff8328f0296af624a6d.sol:
Moles of urea in Solution I $= \text{Molarity} \times \text{Volume in L} = 0.4\text{ mol/L} \times 0.25\text{ L} = 0.1\text{ mol}$.

Mass of urea in Solution I $= 0.1\text{ mol} \times 60\text{ g/mol} = 6\text{ g}$.

Since Solution II contains the same mass of urea, the mass of urea in Solution II is also $6\text{ g}$.

The total mass of Solution II is given as $106\text{ g}$.
Mass of solvent (water) in Solution II $= \text{Mass of solution} - \text{Mass of solute} = 106\text{ g} - 6\text{ g} = 100\text{ g} = 0.1\text{ kg}$.

Molality of Solution II $= \dfrac{\text{Moles of solute}}{\text{Mass of solvent in kg}} = \dfrac{0.1\text{ mol}}{0.1\text{ kg}} = 1.00\text{ m}$.

Answer: $1.00\text{ m}$

6a7a1ff8e920b72a4f09a1f5.subject: Mathematics
6a7a1ff8e920b72a4f09a1f5.text: Let $f(x)$ be a quadratic polynomial with leading coefficient $1$ such that $f(0) = p$, where $p \neq 0$. If the equations $f(x) = 0$ and $f(f(f(x))) = 0$ have a common real root, and $f(p) + f(2) = 6$, then the value of $f(4)$ is ______.
6a7a1ff8e920b72a4f09a1f5.sol:
Let $\alpha$ be the common real root of $f(x) = 0$ and $f(f(f(x))) = 0$.

Since $f(\alpha) = 0$, we have:

$f(f(f(\alpha))) = f(f(0)) = f(p) = 0$.

We are given that $f(p) + f(2) = 6$.

Substituting $f(p) = 0$, we get $0 + f(2) = 6 \Rightarrow f(2) = 6$.

Since $f(p) = 0$, $p$ is a root of the quadratic equation $f(x) = 0$.

Let the roots of $f(x) = 0$ be $p$ and $q$.

Since $f(x)$ is a monic quadratic polynomial, the product of its roots is equal to the constant term $f(0)$.

Thus, $p \cdot q = f(0) = p$.

Since $p \neq 0$, we can divide by $p$ to get $q = 1$.

Therefore, the roots of $f(x) = 0$ are $p$ and $1$, and we can write:

$f(x) = (x - p)(x - 1)$.

Using the condition $f(2) = 6$:

$f(2) = (2 - p)(2 - 1) = 2 - p$.

So, $2 - p = 6 \Rightarrow p = -4$.

The polynomial is $f(x) = (x + 4)(x - 1) = x^2 + 3x - 4$.

We need to find the value of $f(4)$:

$f(4) = (4 + 4)(4 - 1) = 8 \times 3 = 24$.

Answer: $24$

6a7a1ff819f2d42ffcec390b.subject: Mathematics
6a7a1ff819f2d42ffcec390b.text: If the sum of all the solutions of the equation $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1-x}{1+x}\right) + \cot^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1+x}{1-x}\right) = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$, where $x > -1$ and $x \neq 1$, is of the form $\dfrac{k}{\sqrt{3}}$, then the value of $k$ is _____ .
6a7a1ff819f2d42ffcec390b.sol:
Given equation: $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1-x}{1+x}\right) + \cot^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1+x}{1-x}\right) = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ for $x > -1, x \neq 1$.

We know that for $x > -1$, $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1-x}{1+x}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \tan^{-1}x$.

The argument of $\cot^{-1}$ is $\dfrac{1+x}{1-x}$. Since $x > -1$, the numerator $1+x$ is always positive. The sign of the argument depends on $1-x$.

Case 1: Let $x \in (-1, 1)$.
Here, $1-x > 0$, so $\dfrac{1+x}{1-x} > 0$.
Thus, $\cot^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1+x}{1-x}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1-x}{1+x}\right)$.
The equation becomes:
$2\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1-x}{1+x}\right) = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$
$\Rightarrow \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1-x}{1+x}\right) = \dfrac{5\pi}{12}$
$\Rightarrow \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \tan^{-1}x = \dfrac{5\pi}{12}$
$\Rightarrow \tan^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{5\pi}{12} = -\dfrac{\pi}{6}$
$\Rightarrow x = \tan\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$
Since $-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \in (-1, 1)$, this is a valid solution.

Case 2: Let $x > 1$.
Here, $1-x < 0$, so $\dfrac{1+x}{1-x} < 0$.
Thus, $\cot^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1+x}{1-x}\right) = \pi + \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1-x}{1+x}\right)$.
The equation becomes:
$\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1-x}{1+x}\right) + \pi + \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1-x}{1+x}\right) = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$
$\Rightarrow 2\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1-x}{1+x}\right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{6}$
$\Rightarrow \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1-x}{1+x}\right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{12}$
$\Rightarrow \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \tan^{-1}x = -\dfrac{\pi}{12}$
$\Rightarrow \tan^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{\pi}{12} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$
$\Rightarrow x = \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \sqrt{3}$
Since $\sqrt{3} > 1$, this is also a valid solution.

Sum of the solutions = $-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} + \sqrt{3} = \dfrac{-1 + 3}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$.

Comparing with $\dfrac{k}{\sqrt{3}}$, we get $k = 2$.

Answer: $2$

6a7a1ff832e834a1f0fae59a.text: If $\int x \ln x \left( x^{x^2} e^{-\dfrac{x^2}{2}} + x^{-x^2} e^{\dfrac{x^2}{2}} \right) dx = \dfrac{1}{k} \left( x^{\alpha x^2} e^{\beta x^2} - x^{\gamma x^2} e^{\delta x^2} \right) + C$, where $k > 0$ and $C$ is the constant of integration, then the value of $k \cdot |\alpha \beta \gamma \delta|^{-1}$ is
6a7a1ff832e834a1f0fae59a.sol:
Let $I = \int x \ln x \left( x^{x^2} e^{-\dfrac{x^2}{2}} + x^{-x^2} e^{\dfrac{x^2}{2}} \right) dx$

Let $u = x^{x^2} e^{-\dfrac{x^2}{2}}$. Taking the natural logarithm on both sides:
$\ln u = x^2 \ln x - \dfrac{x^2}{2}$

Differentiating with respect to $x$:
$\dfrac{1}{u} \dfrac{du}{dx} = 2x \ln x + x^2 \left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) - x = 2x \ln x + x - x = 2x \ln x$
$\Rightarrow x \ln x \cdot u = \dfrac{1}{2} \dfrac{du}{dx}$

Similarly, let $v = x^{-x^2} e^{\dfrac{x^2}{2}}$. Taking the natural logarithm:
$\ln v = -x^2 \ln x + \dfrac{x^2}{2}$

Differentiating with respect to $x$:
$\dfrac{1}{v} \dfrac{dv}{dx} = -2x \ln x - x^2 \left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) + x = -2x \ln x - x + x = -2x \ln x$
$\Rightarrow x \ln x \cdot v = -\dfrac{1}{2} \dfrac{dv}{dx}$

Substitute these into the integral:
$I = \int \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \dfrac{du}{dx} - \dfrac{1}{2} \dfrac{dv}{dx} \right) dx$
$I = \dfrac{1}{2} (u - v) + C$
$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( x^{x^2} e^{-\dfrac{x^2}{2}} - x^{-x^2} e^{\dfrac{x^2}{2}} \right) + C$

Comparing this with the given expression $\dfrac{1}{k} \left( x^{\alpha x^2} e^{\beta x^2} - x^{\gamma x^2} e^{\delta x^2} \right) + C$, we get:
$k = 2$
$\alpha = 1$, $\beta = -\dfrac{1}{2}$
$\gamma = -1$, $\delta = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Now, calculate the required value:
$|\alpha \beta \gamma \delta| = \left| (1) \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) (-1) \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \right| = \dfrac{1}{4}$

Therefore, $k \cdot |\alpha \beta \gamma \delta|^{-1} = 2 \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{-1} = 2 \cdot 4 = 8$.

Answer: $8$

6a7a1ff8c28d5965de1ac4ad.text: Let $x = f(y)$ be the solution of the differential equation $y \ln y \, dx - (x + y^2 (\ln y)^2) \, dy = 0$ for $y > 1$, satisfying the condition $f(e) = \dfrac{e^2}{2}$. The area of the region bounded by the curve $x = f(y)$, the $y$-axis, and the lines $y = 1$ and $y = e$ is :
6a7a1ff8c28d5965de1ac4ad.sol:
The given differential equation can be rewritten as :
$y \ln y \dfrac{dx}{dy} - x = y^2 (\ln y)^2$
$\Rightarrow \dfrac{dx}{dy} - \dfrac{1}{y \ln y}x = y \ln y$

This is a linear differential equation in $x$. The integrating factor (I.F.) is :
I.F. $= e^{\int -\dfrac{1}{y \ln y} dy} = e^{-\ln(\ln y)} = \dfrac{1}{\ln y}$

Multiplying by the I.F., we get :
$\dfrac{d}{dy}\left(\dfrac{x}{\ln y}\right) = y$

Integrating both sides with respect to $y$ :
$\dfrac{x}{\ln y} = \dfrac{y^2}{2} + C$

Using the initial condition $f(e) = \dfrac{e^2}{2}$, we substitute $x = \dfrac{e^2}{2}$ and $y = e$ :
$\dfrac{\dfrac{e^2}{2}}{\ln e} = \dfrac{e^2}{2} + C \Rightarrow \dfrac{e^2}{2} = \dfrac{e^2}{2} + C \Rightarrow C = 0$

So, the equation of the curve is $x = \dfrac{y^2}{2} \ln y$.

The area bounded by this curve, the $y$-axis ($x=0$), $y=1$, and $y=e$ is given by :
Area $= \int_{1}^{e} x \, dy = \int_{1}^{e} \dfrac{y^2}{2} \ln y \, dy$

We evaluate this integral using integration by parts, letting $u = \ln y$ and $dv = \dfrac{y^2}{2} dy$ :
$\int \dfrac{y^2}{2} \ln y \, dy = (\ln y)\left(\dfrac{y^3}{6}\right) - \int \dfrac{1}{y} \cdot \dfrac{y^3}{6} \, dy$
$= \dfrac{y^3}{6} \ln y - \int \dfrac{y^2}{6} \, dy = \dfrac{y^3}{6} \ln y - \dfrac{y^3}{18}$

Applying the limits from $1$ to $e$ :
Area $= \left[ \dfrac{e^3}{6} \ln e - \dfrac{e^3}{18} \right] - \left[ \dfrac{1^3}{6} \ln 1 - \dfrac{1^3}{18} \right]$
Area $= \left( \dfrac{e^3}{6} - \dfrac{e^3}{18} \right) - \left( 0 - \dfrac{1}{18} \right)$
Area $= \dfrac{2e^3}{18} + \dfrac{1}{18} = \dfrac{2e^3 + 1}{18}$

Answer: $\dfrac{2e^3 + 1}{18}$

6a7a1ff8f7f179919dcbca63.text: Let $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ be two vectors such that $|\vec{a}| = 1$, $|\vec{b}| = 2$ and $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} > 0$. If the area of the parallelogram adjacent sides of which are represented by the vectors $\vec{p} = 2\vec{a} + \vec{b}$ and $\vec{q} = \vec{a} - 2\vec{b}$ is $5\sqrt{3}$, and the vectors $\vec{u} = \lambda \vec{a} + \vec{b}$ and $\vec{v} = 2\vec{a} - \lambda \vec{b}$ are perpendicular to each other, then the value of $\lambda^2 + 2\lambda$ is :
6a7a1ff8f7f179919dcbca63.sol:
The area of the parallelogram is given by $|\vec{p} \times \vec{q}|$.

$\vec{p} \times \vec{q} = (2\vec{a} + \vec{b}) \times (\vec{a} - 2\vec{b})$
$= 2(\vec{a} \times \vec{a}) - 4(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) + (\vec{b} \times \vec{a}) - 2(\vec{b} \times \vec{b})$
$= \vec{0} - 4(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) - (\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) - \vec{0} = -5(\vec{a} \times \vec{b})$

Given the area is $5\sqrt{3}$:
$|-5(\vec{a} \times \vec{b})| = 5\sqrt{3} \Rightarrow 5|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\sin\theta = 5\sqrt{3}$
$5(1)(2)\sin\theta = 5\sqrt{3} \Rightarrow \sin\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

Since $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} > 0$, $\cos\theta > 0$, so $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
Thus, $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta = (1)(2)\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 1$.

Now, $\vec{u}$ and $\vec{v}$ are perpendicular, so $\vec{u} \cdot \vec{v} = 0$:
$(\lambda \vec{a} + \vec{b}) \cdot (2\vec{a} - \lambda \vec{b}) = 0$
$2\lambda|\vec{a}|^2 - \lambda^2(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}) + 2(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}) - \lambda|\vec{b}|^2 = 0$

Substitute the known values:
$2\lambda(1)^2 - \lambda^2(1) + 2(1) - \lambda(2)^2 = 0$
$2\lambda - \lambda^2 + 2 - 4\lambda = 0$
$-\lambda^2 - 2\lambda + 2 = 0$
$\lambda^2 + 2\lambda = 2$

Answer: $2$

6a7a1ff8029a054291ff92cf.text: If the length of the perpendicular drawn from the point $P(\alpha, 3, 5)$, where $\alpha > 2$, on the line $\dfrac{x-1}{1} = \dfrac{y-2}{1} = \dfrac{z-3}{1}$ is $\sqrt{2}$ units, and $\Pi$ is the plane containing the point $P$ and the given line, then the square of the perpendicular distance of the point $A(5, 4, 3)$ from the plane $\Pi$ is equal to
6a7a1ff8029a054291ff92cf.sol:
Let a point on the line $\dfrac{x-1}{1} = \dfrac{y-2}{1} = \dfrac{z-3}{1} = \lambda$ be $M(\lambda+1, \lambda+2, \lambda+3)$.

The direction ratios of the line are $\langle 1, 1, 1 \rangle$.

The direction ratios of the line segment joining $P(\alpha, 3, 5)$ and $M$ are $\langle \lambda+1-\alpha, \lambda-1, \lambda-2 \rangle$.

Since $PM$ is perpendicular to the given line:
$1(\lambda+1-\alpha) + 1(\lambda-1) + 1(\lambda-2) = 0$
$\Rightarrow 3\lambda - \alpha - 2 = 0 \Rightarrow \lambda = \dfrac{\alpha+2}{3}$

The square of the distance $PM$ is $2$:
$(\lambda+1-\alpha)^2 + (\lambda-1)^2 + (\lambda-2)^2 = 2$

Substituting $\lambda = \dfrac{\alpha+2}{3}$:
$\left(\dfrac{5-2\alpha}{3}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\alpha-1}{3}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\alpha-4}{3}\right)^2 = 2$
$\Rightarrow (25 - 20\alpha + 4\alpha^2) + (\alpha^2 - 2\alpha + 1) + (\alpha^2 - 8\alpha + 16) = 18$
$\Rightarrow 6\alpha^2 - 30\alpha + 42 = 18$
$\Rightarrow 6\alpha^2 - 30\alpha + 24 = 0$
$\Rightarrow \alpha^2 - 5\alpha + 4 = 0$
$\Rightarrow (\alpha-1)(\alpha-4) = 0$

Since $\alpha > 2$, we have $\alpha = 4$. Thus, $P$ is $(4, 3, 5)$.

The plane $\Pi$ contains the line and the point $P$. A point on the line is $B(1, 2, 3)$.
Vector $\vec{BP} = 3\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$.

The normal vector to the plane $\Pi$ is $\vec{n} = \vec{BP} \times \vec{d} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 3 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = -\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$.

The equation of the plane $\Pi$ is $-1(x-1) - 1(y-2) + 2(z-3) = 0 \Rightarrow x + y - 2z + 3 = 0$.

The perpendicular distance of $A(5, 4, 3)$ from the plane $\Pi$ is:
$d = \dfrac{|5 + 4 - 2(3) + 3|}{\sqrt{1^2 + 1^2 + (-2)^2}} = \dfrac{6}{\sqrt{6}} = \sqrt{6}$.

The square of the distance is $d^2 = 6$.

Answer: $6$
